posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

Death isn't a single switch that shuts down your entire body at once. When your heart stops beating and your brain goes silent, trillions of cells inside you are still alive, desperately trying to keep themselves running. Death isn't a single moment, but a slow and surprisingly complex process that can last for weeks.

What actually happens when you die? What makes death so mysterious, and which cells are the last survivors within your body? Watch our full video to find out!

recentPosts.caption:
@antronoid captured London’s Tower Bridge at 7 a.m. as thick fog rolled over the city.⁠
⁠
Lights from passing traffic streaked across the bridge, and just at the right moment, flocks of birds flew straight through the frame. ⁠
⁠
This is a real photo, not AI! Just perfect timing and a lucky morning. 📸

A journey of faith, one step at a time. 🙏⛰️ At Tirumala in India, many devotees choose to climb around 3,550 steps to reach the sacred Tirupati Balaji Temple. ⁠
⁠
For them, every step is an act of devotion, making the climb just as meaningful as reaching the destination. ❤️⁠
🎥: @_swatiiiiii_13

With its dark skin speckled in blue and patches of bright orange, it’s easy to see how the galaxy frog got its name. These tiny frogs grow to only about an inch long and live in the wet forests of India’s southern Western Ghats, where they tend to hide under rotting logs.⁠
⁠
Photographer @hadlee_renjith captured these close-ups in Munnar, Kerala. The galaxy frog is listed as Vulnerable, as it lives in a small range and is very sensitive to heat, drying out and disturbance.⁠
⁠

A room built from the remains of the dead, and still standing more than 800 years later. 💀⁠
Hidden beside the Basilica of Santo Stefano in Milan, the San Bernardino alle Ossa ossuary was built in 1210 to house bones displaced from the cemetery of the nearby Brolo Hospital. ⁠
⁠
Its walls became a resting place for thousands of remains, belonging to patients, hospital staff, clergy and others.Despite fires, collapses and centuries of rebuilding around it, the ossuary survived. A fascinating, eeri

A brush fire was heading straight for Aaron’s home while he was at work. His wife Sarah was asleep and her phone was off, so he opened his @Ring app and used Two-Way Talk to wake her up. Sarah made it out safely, and firefighters arrived just in time to stop the blaze!

High in the Daisetsuzan Mountains of Hokkaido, the wind was so strong that it parted this little pika’s fur. Even so, the pika didn’t seem to mind. It kept eating, running around and calling out energetically through the gusts.⁠
⁠
By: @fujikofujio2023

Who knew charging your phone at the airport could double as a workout? 😂🔋 ⁠
Berlin Airport has a pretty genius solution: pedal your way to a full battery! A little movement, some free energy and no more hunting for an empty socket. 🚴‍♀️⁠
🎥: @running.bibii

The Shady Dell first opened in 1927 as a stop for travelers on U.S. Highway 80, one of America’s early cross-country routes. Nearly a century later, it still welcomes road trippers, with a lot more retro charm.⁠
⁠
Instead of standard hotel rooms, guests stay in restored vintage trailers, each with its own personality. ⁠
⁠
Inside, you’ll find pastel kitchens, wood-paneled walls, record players, and old-school TVs, all carefully preserved to capture the spirit of classic American road trips.

A beautiful tradition of respect and appreciation. ❤️ ⁠
During Bhai Tika in Nepal, women are honored by their brothers and male family members, who touch their feet and offer blessings and gifts as a gesture of love, gratitude and respect. ⁠
⁠
The ritual reflects a cultural belief in the importance of women in bringing prosperity and good fortune to the family.⁠
🎥: @sanjushreshtha

These lagoons look like they were painted onto the salt. 💛⁠
⁠
Salar de Gorbea in Chile is known for its striking yellow, green, and turquoise lagoons, set against huge stretches of white salt and reddish volcanic mountains.⁠
⁠
The colors come from the minerals, microorganisms, high salt concentrations, and volcanic activity found in this remote part of the Atacama.⁠
⁠
Getting here isn’t easy either. Salar de Gorbea sits at nearly 4,000 meters above sea level and is usually visited as part of a

In this Romanian bar, ordering a shot comes with a little extra surprise: a keg to the head! 🍻😂 ⁠
Don't worry, they provide a helmet… because apparently, that's part of the experience.⁠
🎥: @sarmiswilldoit

Le Train Bleu, @restaurantletrainbleu, inside Gare de Lyon station in Paris is a restaurant that looks more like a palace than a place to wait for your train.⁠
⁠
It was created for the 1900 World’s Fair, and its dining rooms are covered with 41 paintings, many showing the French destinations travelers could reach by train. With gold details, chandeliers and painted ceilings, it’s been a historic monument since 1972.⁠
⁠
Would you come here for lunch even if you weren’t catching a train?

National Geographic photographers ventured to places far and wide to capture the year’s most fascinating images. Out of millions of photos, just 25 were selected as our Pictures of the Year. 

We thought these photos of a juvenile Greenland shark, possibly born around the time of the American Civil War, a climber dangling from a horizontal ledge in Spain during August’s solar eclipse, and an astronaut training for a lunar mission managed to capture the vastness of both time and space, all in a f

Presented by National Geographic Society in partnership with @Rolex. 

When corals get too hot, they can lose the algae that help keep them alive, causing them to bleach. Could some naturally heat-tolerant corals hold the key to the future of our reefs? National Geographic Explorer Dr. Anya Brown and her team are trying to find out exactly that.

Rolex and The National Geographic Society are partnering on select science-based expeditions to explore, study, and document change in the planet’s unique regions. #PerpetualPlanet. 

Note: Footage from the Southern Ocean taken during the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Southern Ocean Exped

Drawn to the light filtering through its ice formations, photographer Christoph Johann (@johann_photography) explored Alaska's Sheridan Glacier alongside skier Simon Hillis. His goal was to capture unexpected perspectives of the landscape, something he believes can happen when you step off the beaten path and into another world.

See more Photos of the Day at the link in bio.

Let it snow, let it sparkle, let the world slow down for a moment ❄️

#WildYellowstone is now streaming on @DisneyPlus.

Presented by National Geographic Society in partnership with @Rolex.

Pygmy blue whales compete with fin whales for the title of the second-largest animal in the world. They typically roam the world’s oceans, but one group off the coast of New Zealand seems to have settled in the South Taranaki Bight. To better understand the behavior of these marine giants, researchers are studying some of the ocean’s smallest creatures—swarms of krill thriving in the whales’ new home. They hope that by underst

Photo by @joelsartore | This brightly colored serpent is an ornate palm pit viper that I photographed @sanantoniozoo. In the wild, the species can be found in the cloud forests of Mexico and northern Guatemala. Unfortunately, this snake’s habitat is used frequently for agricultural purposes—growing coffee plants and ornamental ferns—which has decreased suitable habitat. You can do your part to protect the snake by purchasing wildlife-friendly coffee and growing plants native to your region in yo

Indris are the largest lemur species in the world, and they are known for their astonishingly loud, musical singing. Found in Madagascar, indris are among the many animals unique to the island—but their habitat is threatened. Now, to estimate the population, scientists are using a process known as passive acoustic monitoring to map the density and abundance of the endemic species.

Learn more about the efforts to protect indris at the link in bio. 

Video by Ethology Lab at the University of Tur

There’s more than slime hiding in this tar pit! Unearth the woolly mammoth, assemble its bones, and bring your prehistoric discovery to life—it even glows in the dark.

Available now on Amazon at the link in bio.

Presented by National Geographic Society in partnership with @Rolex.

The extreme temperatures of a hydrothermal vent may not seem ideal for life, but a host of organisms can be found in this mineral-rich environment—and, for the first time, scientists have observed Antarctic krill among them.

This was part of the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Southern Ocean Expedition conducted in collaboration with the Schmidt Ocean Institute aboard their research vessel Falkor (too).

Rolex

The ketogenic diet has helped some people find relief from chronic migraines, but its restrictive nature and potential health risks make it a controversial treatment. Now, researchers are looking more closely at how rapid swings in blood sugar, which standard tests may miss, could play a role. While some patients respond better to the diet than others, experts hope their findings could lead to more personalized treatment options.

Learn more at the link in bio.

Illustration by NGM Staff; Photog
